steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a theory paper on reinforcement learning from preference-based (human) feedback. It should explain why current RLHF lacks a usable theoretical foundation, bring in query complexity as a second concern, and summarize our randomization-based algorithms and contributions, ending with the practical takeaways.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- RLHF and why feedback comes as preferences
- Gap between empirical RLHF and theory
- Query complexity: human feedback is expensive
- Our goal and key idea: randomization
- Contributions: linear MDP algorithm, Thompson sampling for general function approximation, variance-based query condition
- Practical insights from the theory

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- RLHF and preferences
  - used in robotics and NLP (cite)
  - unlike standard RL: preferences between pairs of trajectories, not per-step reward
  - dense reward per state hard to assign; e.g. rating each generated token in NL generation
  - more realistic: humans compare two pieces of text, indicate preference
  - recent works: preference feedback in training -> align models with human intention, high-quality human-machine interaction
- Theory gap
  - practice: learn reward model from preferences, then optimize with policy-gradient methods like PPO (cite)
  - ignored questions: is learned reward model accurate? is PPO enough for deep exploration? how to collect more feedback strategically on the fly?
  - theory: regret bounds for RL with preference feedback (cite)
  - sublinear worst-case regret but computationally intractable, even tabular MDPs
  - so their algorithmic ideas can't guide/improve RLHF in practice
- Query complexity
  - human feedback expensive -> second metric besides reward
  - InstructGPT: only 30K instances of human feedback (cite) vs internet-scale data for GPT-3 base model
  - hard to scale human feedback datasets
  - prior works: extensive querying burdens human experts (cite)
  - empirical: active learning reduces query complexity, improves reward model (cite)
  - theory: studied in active learning, online learning, bandits (cite); overlooked in RL
- Goal + key idea
  - RL from preference feedback efficient in regret, computation, query complexity
  - near-optimal balance between regret and query complexity
  - key idea: randomization
- Contributions
  - linear MDP (cite): first algorithm with sublinear worst-case regret + computational efficiency under preference feedback; also first for tabular; active learning, near-optimal regret/query tradeoff
  - random Gaussian noise on state-action-wise reward model and LSVI; instead of UCB-style (cite) -> keeps Markovian property -> dynamic programming
  - beyond linear: model-based Thompson sampling, posteriors over transitions and reward models
  - assumption: small \ell_{1} -norm eluder dimension (cite), more general than \ell_{2} -norm (cite); near-optimal Bayesian regret vs Bayesian query complexity
  - computation: Bayesian supervised learning oracles, like earlier TS for regular RL (cite)
  - query condition: variance-style uncertainty of preference from randomness of reward model; query only when uncertainty large; approximate with i.i.d. random reward models
- Practical insights
  - main contribution theoretical, but new practical insights
  - pair of trajectories: one from latest policy, one from older policy, not both from same policy (cite) -> avoids similar trajectories as policy becomes deterministic; better exploration/exploitation
  - variance-style uncertainty vs version space / confidence intervals (cite): strong guarantees, more tractable
  - fits existing TS RL implementations, e.g. bootstrapping for posterior sampling (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) is used a lot in many domains, for example robotics and natural language processing. In standard RL the agent gets a reward at every step, but in RLHF the agent has to learn from feedback that comes as preferences between pairs of trajectories. The reason is that in many tasks it is hard to assign a dense reward function for every state. For example, in natural language generation it is hard to rate each generated token on its own, so it is more realistic to ask humans to compare two pieces of text and say which one they prefer. Recent works have shown that if we integrate preference-based feedback into training, we can align models with human intention and get high-quality human-machine interaction.

But even though RLHF is used a lot empirically, its theoretical foundation is still far from satisfactory. In practice, researchers first learn reward models from the preference-based feedback, and then they optimize the reward models with policy gradient-based algorithms like PPO. Some questions are often ignored, like whether the learned reward model is accurate, whether PPO is enough for deep exploration, and how to strategically collect more feedback on the fly. On the theory side, prior works study the regret bound for RL with preference-based feedback. These algorithms get sublinear worst-case regret, but they are computationally intractable, even for simplified models like tabular Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). So we cannot easily use the algorithmic ideas of prior work to guide or improve how RLHF is done in practice.

Besides maximizing reward, query complexity is another important metric in RLHF, because human feedback is expensive to collect. For example, the training data of InstructGPT has only 30K instances of human feedback, which is much less than the internet-scale dataset used to train the GPT-3 base model. This shows that scaling up the size of human feedback datasets is a challenge. Other works also pointed out that querying a lot for feedback puts too much burden on human experts. Empirically, one work observes that active learning reduces query complexity and also improves the learned reward model. In theory, query complexity is mostly studied in active learning, online learning and bandits, but it is overlooked in RL.

- Goal + key idea
  - RL algorithms learning from preference feedback, efficient in regret, computation and query complexity
  - near-optimal balance between regret minimization and query complexity minimization
  - key idea: randomization in algorithm design
- Contributions
  - linear MDP: first algorithm with sublinear worst-case regret + computational efficiency with preference feedback; also first for tabular MDPs; active learning, near-optimal regret/query tradeoff
  - random Gaussian noise on state-action-wise reward model and LSVI instead of UCB-style -> keeps Markovian property -> dynamic programming
  - beyond linear: model-based Thompson sampling over transitions and reward models; small \ell_{1} -norm eluder dimension (more general than \ell_{2} -norm); near-optimal Bayesian regret vs Bayesian query complexity; Bayesian supervised learning oracles
  - query condition: variance-style uncertainty of preference; query only when large; approximate with i.i.d. random reward models
- Practical insights
  - pair of trajectories from latest + older policy instead of same policy; avoids similar trajectories; better exploration/exploitation
  - variance-style uncertainty vs version space and confidence intervals: guarantees + tractable
  - fits TS RL implementations (bootstrapping for posterior sampling)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) is used a lot in many domains, for example robotics and natural language processing. In standard RL the agent gets a reward at every step, but in RLHF the agent has to learn from feedback that comes as preferences between pairs of trajectories. The reason is that in many tasks it is hard to assign a dense reward function for every state. For example, in natural language generation it is hard to rate each generated token on its own, so it is more realistic to ask humans to compare two pieces of text and say which one they prefer. Recent works have shown that if we integrate preference-based feedback into training, we can align models with human intention and get high-quality human-machine interaction.

But even though RLHF is used a lot empirically, its theoretical foundation is still far from satisfactory. In practice, researchers first learn reward models from the preference-based feedback, and then they optimize the reward models with policy gradient-based algorithms like PPO. Some questions are often ignored, like whether the learned reward model is accurate, whether PPO is enough for deep exploration, and how to strategically collect more feedback on the fly. On the theory side, prior works study the regret bound for RL with preference-based feedback. These algorithms get sublinear worst-case regret, but they are computationally intractable, even for simplified models like tabular Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). So we cannot easily use the algorithmic ideas of prior work to guide or improve how RLHF is done in practice.

Besides maximizing reward, query complexity is another important metric in RLHF, because human feedback is expensive to collect. For example, the training data of InstructGPT has only 30K instances of human feedback, which is much less than the internet-scale dataset used to train the GPT-3 base model. This shows that scaling up the size of human feedback datasets is a challenge. Other works also pointed out that querying a lot for feedback puts too much burden on human experts. Empirically, one work observes that active learning reduces query complexity and also improves the learned reward model. In theory, query complexity is mostly studied in active learning, online learning and bandits, but it is overlooked in RL.

In this work we want to design new RL algorithms that learn from preference-based feedback and are efficient in statistical complexity (i.e., regret), computational complexity, and query complexity. In particular, we get a near-optimal balance between regret minimization and query complexity minimization. Our key idea for this is to use randomization in the algorithm design. Our new algorithmic ideas and key contributions are the following.

- 1. For MDPs with linear structure (i.e., linear MDP), we propose the first RL algorithm with preference-based feedback that gets sublinear worst-case regret and is computationally efficient at the same time. Even for tabular MDPs, it is the first one with a no-regret guarantee and computational efficiency. It also has an active learning procedure and gets a near-optimal tradeoff between the regret and the query complexity. The algorithm adds random Gaussian noises to the learned state-action-wise reward model and to the least-squares value iteration (LSVI) procedure. We use random noise instead of the UCB-style technique because it keeps the Markovian property in the reward model, and this lets us use dynamic programming to be computationally efficient.

- 2. For function approximation beyond linear, we give a model-based Thompson-sampling (TS) algorithm that forms posterior distributions over the transitions and the reward models. We assume the transition and the reward model class both have small \ell_{1} -norm eluder dimension, which is a structural condition introduced in prior work and is more general than the common \ell_{2} -norm eluder dimension. Under this assumption we show that the algorithm again gets a near-optimal tradeoff between the Bayesian regret and the Bayesian query complexity. For computation, the main computation primitives are Bayesian supervised learning oracles for transition and reward learning, the same as in previous TS algorithms for regular RL.

- 3. For both algorithms, the query conditions are based on a variance-style uncertainty quantification of the preference, which comes from the randomness of the reward model. We only query for preference feedback when the uncertainty of the preference on a pair of trajectories is large. The uncertainty can be computed approximately in an easy way with i.i.d. random reward models drawn from the reward model distribution, so the active query procedure is computationally tractable.

Our main contribution is theoretical, but the theoretical investigation also gives several new practical insights. For example, for regret minimization our algorithms draw a pair of trajectories where one is from the latest policy and the other is from an older policy, instead of drawing both trajectories from the same policy as earlier work does. This avoids drawing two similar trajectories when the policy becomes more and more deterministic. Our theory shows that drawing the two trajectories from a combination of new and older policies balances exploration and exploitation better. Another practical insight is the variance-style uncertainty measure for the query condition. Compared to the more standard active learning procedure that relies on constructing version space and confidence intervals, our approach has strong theoretical guarantees and is more computationally tractable. It also works with existing implementations of Thompson sampling RL algorithms, for example using bootstrapping to approximate the posterior sampling.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has been widely used across various domains, including robotics [1,2] and natural language processing [3,4]. Unlike standard RL, RLHF requires the agent to learn from feedback in the form of preferences between pairs of trajectories instead of per-step reward, since assigning a dense reward function for each state is challenging in many tasks. For instance, in natural language generation, it is hard to rate each generated token individually. It is therefore more realistic to ask humans to compare two pieces of text and indicate which they prefer. Recent works have shown that, by integrating preference-based feedback into the training process, we can align models with human intention and enable high-quality human-machine interaction.

Despite these empirical applications of RLHF, its theoretical foundation remains far from satisfactory. Empirically, researchers first learn reward models from preference-based feedback and then optimize them via policy gradient-based algorithms such as PPO [5]. Questions such as whether the learned reward model is accurate, whether PPO is sufficient for deep exploration, and how to strategically collect more feedback on the fly are often ignored. Theoretically, prior works study the regret bound for RL with preference-based feedback [6,7]. Although these algorithms achieve sublinear worst-case regret, they are computationally intractable even for simplified models such as tabular Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). This means we cannot easily leverage the algorithmic ideas of prior work to guide or improve how RLHF is performed in practice.

In addition to maximizing reward, another important metric in RLHF is query complexity, since human feedback is expensive to collect. To illustrate, InstructGPT's training data comprises a mere 30K instances of human feedback [4], significantly fewer than the internet-scale dataset used to train the GPT-3 base model. This underscores the challenge of scaling up human feedback datasets. [8,9] also pointed out that extensive querying for feedback places too much burden on human experts. Empirically, [10] observes that active learning reduces query complexity and improves the learned reward model. In theory, query complexity has mostly been studied in the settings of active learning, online learning, and bandits [11,12,13,14,15,16,17], but it has been overlooked in RL.

In this work, we aim to design new RL algorithms that learn from preference-based feedback and are efficient in statistical complexity (i.e., regret), computational complexity, and query complexity. In particular, we strike a near-optimal balance between regret minimization and query complexity minimization. Our key idea for achieving this is to use randomization in algorithm design. We summarize our new algorithmic ideas and key contributions as follows.

- 1. For MDPs with linear structure (i.e., linear MDP [18]), we propose the first RL algorithm with preference-based feedback that achieves sublinear worst-case regret and computational efficiency simultaneously. Even when reduced to tabular MDPs, it is still the first to achieve a no-regret guarantee together with computational efficiency. - 2. For function approximation beyond linear, we present a model-based Thompson-sampling (TS) algorithm that forms posterior distributions over the transitions and reward models. Assuming that the transition and reward model classes both have small \ell_{1} -norm eluder dimension – a structural condition introduced in [20] that is more general than the common \ell_{2} -norm eluder dimension [21] – we show that our algorithm again achieves a near-optimal tradeoff between the Bayesian regret and the Bayesian query complexity. Computation-wise, as in previous TS algorithms for regular RL (e.g., [22]), the primary computation primitives are Bayesian supervised learning oracles for transition and reward learning.

- 3. The query conditions of both algorithms are based on a variance-style uncertainty quantification of the preference, induced by the randomness of the reward model. We query for preference feedback only when the uncertainty of the preference on a pair of trajectories is large. The uncertainty can be approximately computed with i.i.d. random reward models drawn from the reward model distribution, which makes the active query procedure computationally tractable.

Overall, while our main contribution is theoretical, our theoretical investigation provides several new practical insights. For instance, for regret minimization, our algorithms draw a pair of trajectories with one from the latest policy and the other from an older policy, instead of drawing both from the same policy (e.g., [23]); this avoids drawing two similar trajectories as the policy becomes more and more deterministic. Our theory shows that drawing the two trajectories from a combination of new and older policies better balances exploration and exploitation. Another practical insight is the variance-style uncertainty measure used to design the query condition. Compared to the more standard active learning procedure that relies on constructing version spaces and confidence intervals [12,24,15,16,17], our approach comes with strong theoretical guarantees and is more computationally tractable. It is also amenable to existing implementations of Thompson sampling RL algorithms (e.g., using bootstrapping to approximate the posterior sampling [25,26]).
